content.text: The sum of residuals is constrained to zero in a standard regression model with an intercept, but this constraint is lifted in a no-intercept model. Forcing a regression line through the origin when a non-zero intercept exists introduces significant specification bias. Need to solidify the foundational understanding further.

The search is restricted to publications from November 2026 or earlier. The goal is to find foundational and survey literature to support using transparent prediction-error calculations in teaching.

Pedagogical literature on teaching regression, omitted intercepts, and residuals is being reviewed. Specifically, works by Eisenhauer (2003), Becker & Kennedy (1992), and Hahn (1977) are being considered. These papers will help in demonstrating how residuals behave when an intercept is excluded versus included in regression, and other pedagogical misconceptions. The goal is to provide a solid foundation for the explanation within the teaching note.

Examining literature focused on specification bias resulting from omitting a non-zero constant and the corresponding non-zero residual sum. Papers by Hawkins (1980), Casella (1983), Anscombe (1973), and Kvalseth (1985) offer relevant pedagogical insights into intercept omission and residual behavior. The goal is to select sources that are useful for understanding how these residuals behave within regression.

Reviewing Friedman's (2001) work on Gradient Boosting Machines and Friedman, Hastie, & Tibshirani (2000) additive logistic regression to understand foundational concepts connecting prediction error/residual calculation to additive corrections. These sources will inform the use of prediction error in teaching.

Examined literature linking machine learning boosting and statistical estimation through additive residual fitting. Found several key sources providing overviews of boosting algorithms, additive models, and the use of residuals for correction, including Bühlmann & Hothorn (2007), Mayr et al. (2014), Natekin & Knoll (2013), Hastie & Tibshirani (1986), and Schapire (2003). These sources illustrate how prediction errors are iteratively addressed with additive terms.
